parole.significato: Master of the house, head of the household, host.

parole.significato: mistress of the house
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish בעל־הביתטע (baleboste), feminine form of בעל־הבית (balebos), from Hebrew בַּעַל הַבַּיִת (bá'al habáyit, “master of the house”).

parole.significato: preordained, fated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish באַשערט (bashert), from Middle High German beschern. Compare German bescheren.

parole.significato: A kiddush cup
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish בעכער (bekher, “goblet”). Doublet of beaker and pitcher.

parole.significato: A black frock coat worn by Hassidim.

parole.significato: To recite the Birkat Hamazon.

parole.significato: A booklet containing grace after meals and often other blessings and prayers related to mealtime.

parole.testo: From Yiddish ביאַלי (byali), from the Polish name of the city of Białystok.

parole.significato: A small amount; a bit.
parole.testo: From Yiddish ביסל (bisl); cognate with the homologous Germanic-language words Bissel, Bisslein, and Bisschen, as well as English bit.

parole.significato: A metal sheet used to cover stovetop burners on Shabbat to allow food to be kept warm without violating the prohibition…
parole.testo: From Yiddish בלעך (blekh). Related to German Blech.

parole.significato: A thin blin (pancake), filled (often with sweet cheese) and folded, then fried and often served with sour cream, fruit,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish בלינצע (blintse).

parole.significato: A beetroot soup that can be served hot or cold, usually with sour cream, called borsch in its countries of origin.
parole.testo: 1884 or 1808. Borrowed from Yiddish באָרשט (borsht), from Russian or Ukrainian борщ (boršč). Doublet of barszcz.

parole.significato: Term of endearment for a young boy, or a young man.
parole.testo: From American Yiddish בויטשיק (boytshik), from a blend of English boy + Russian ма́льчик (málʹčik, “boy”).

parole.significato: Blessing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ברכה (brokhe), from Hebrew בְּרָכָה (b'rakhá).

parole.significato: Angry or resentful.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ברוגז (broyges), from Hebrew ברוגז \ בְּרֹגֶז (literally “in anger, with anger”).

parole.significato: A knife used by Ashkenazi Jews in shehitah, the kosher slaughter of animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish חלף (khalaf), from Hebrew חַלָּף (khaláf).

parole.significato: Help! Catch him/her/them!
parole.testo: From Yiddish כאַפּטסעם (khaptsem), from כאַפּן (khapn, “to catch, get”) and אים (im, “him”).

parole.significato: A wedding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish חתונה (khasene), from Hebrew חתונה /חֲתֻנָּה (khatuná).

parole.significato: A pig.

parole.significato: Junk; trash; anything worthless.

parole.testo: Calque of Yiddish ביליק ווי באָרשט (bilik vi borsht), as the beets used to make it were among the cheapest vegetables.

parole.significato: An elementary school for Jewish children, teaching basic Judaism and Hebrew.
parole.testo: From Yiddish חדר (kheyder), from Hebrew חֶדֶר (khéder, “room”).

parole.significato: Certain animal fats that the Torah prohibits Jews and Israelites from eating.
parole.testo: From Yiddish חלבֿ (kheylev), from Hebrew חֵלֶב (khélev).

parole.significato: A wise and learned man
parole.testo: From Yiddish חכם (khokhem), from Hebrew חָכָם (khakhám, “wise, smart”).

parole.significato: A meat and/or bean stew traditionally served on the Sabbath by Jews.
parole.testo: From Yiddish טשאָלנט (tsholnt), of unknown origin, but may be from an Old French reflex of Latin calēns.

parole.significato: A relish in Ashkenazi Jewish cuisine, consisting of grated horseradish, vinegar, sugar, salt, and optionally beetroot.

parole.significato: A fried dumpling made of matzo meal and filled with fruit, typically prunes, and eaten on Passover.
parole.testo: From Yiddish כרעמזל (khremzl).

parole.significato: Showing chutzpah; not showing due respect; impudent; impertinent; brazen.

parole.significato: Clothing; clothes.
parole.testo: British slang from 19th century of unknown origin, perhaps from Yiddish.

parole.significato: to recite the Jewish liturgy; to pray

parole.significato: A gathering of Hassidic Jews for the purpose of inspiring each other in religion and spirituality.

parole.significato: Small pellet-shaped egg pasta in Ashkenazic Jewish cuisine, made instead out of matzah during Passover.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פֿאַרפֿל (farfl).

parole.significato: A fussy or picky person; a connoisseur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פֿײַנשמעקער (faynshmeker). Compare German Feinschmecker (“gourmet”).

parole.significato: An expression of disgust or contempt.

parole.significato: A little bird.

parole.significato: A five-dollar bill (note).

parole.significato: A five-pound (£5) note; the sum of five pounds.

parole.significato: Synonym of p'tcha (“calves'-foot jelly”).

parole.significato: A certain cut of beef used in Ashkenazic Jewish cuisine, made by cutting short ribs across the bone

parole.significato: Meaty, containing meat.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פֿרום (frum, “pious”). Related to German fromm and Dutch vroom.

parole.significato: A Jew who is frum (pious and observant of Jewish laws and customs).
parole.testo: From Yiddish פֿרומער [ייִד] (frumer [yid], “pious [Jew]”).

parole.significato: Synonym of fumfer (“to speak awkwardly or evasively; to fiddle or fumble”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פֿאָנפֿען (fonfen, “to speak with a nasal twang, to mumble”). Compare fumfer.

parole.significato: Pound sterling: the currency of Great Britain; money generally.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פֿונט (funt, “pound (unit of weight)”). Doublet of pfund, pood, pound, and punt.

parole.significato: A Jew of Galician ancestry.

parole.significato: A thief; a rascal or scoundrel.
parole.testo: From Yiddish גנבֿ (ganef), from Hebrew גנב (ganáv, “thief”).

parole.significato: A belt or sash used in prayer.
parole.testo: From Yiddish גאַרטל (gartl). Doublet of girdle.

parole.significato: To swindle; to extort.

parole.significato: Originally, a dish of stuffed fish with the skin intact.

parole.significato: A mixture of various things, a melange.
parole.testo: From Yiddish געמיש (gemish, “mixture”), cognate to German Gemisch.

parole.significato: A business deal.

parole.significato: To subscribe to (an idea , rule, authority, etc.); to personally consider valid or authoritative.

parole.significato: A gunshot wound to the head.

parole.significato: An Ashkenazi Jewish confection made with honey and ginger.
parole.testo: From Yiddish אינגבערלעך (ingberlekh), from אינגבער (ingber, “ginger”).

parole.significato: Synonym of doikeyt.
parole.testo: A semantic loan from Yiddish דאָיִקייט (doikeyt, from דאָיִק (doik, “here or local”) + ־קייט (-keyt, “-ness”)).

parole.significato: A dish of lokshen and kasha.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קאַשע וואַרנישקעס (kashe varnishkes)

parole.significato: To render kosher.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish כּשרן (kashern), from כּשר (kosher, “kosher”).

parole.significato: to observe the rules of kashrut (Jewish dietary laws)
parole.testo: Partial calque of Yiddish האַלטן כּשר (haltn kosher, “to keep kosher”).

parole.significato: camaraderie or solidarity
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish חבֿרשאַפֿט (khavershaft).

parole.significato: A pig; a greedy person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish חזיר (khazer), from Hebrew חֲזִיר.

parole.significato: A boy or lad; a rascal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish כוואַט (khvat)

parole.significato: To make small talk or idle chatter.
parole.testo: From Yiddish קיבעצן (kibetsn), cognate to German kiebitzen (“to look on”), from German Kiebitz (“lapwing”), from Middle High German gibiz (“plover”), imitative of its cry. Compare peewit.

parole.significato: a sweet cracker or cookie in Jewish cuisine
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קיכל (kikhl).

parole.significato: A Jew.
parole.testo: Originally used by German-American Jews as a slur for Eastern European Jews immigrating to the United States. The most dominant theory is from Yiddish קײַקל (kaykl, “circle”). In the early 20th century, non-English-speaking Jews that immigrated to the United States would sign papers with a circle as

parole.significato: A dish made from stuffed intestine.
parole.testo: Attested in English since the late 1930s, from Yiddish קישקע (kishke), from Slavic—Polish kiszka, Russian кишка́ (kišká), or Ukrainian ки́шка (kýška). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kyšьka (“intestine, stomach”). May be related to Sanskrit कोष्ठ (koṣṭha, “intestine”) or Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis,

parole.significato: A white linen or cotton robe worn by religious Ashkenazi Jews on holidays, in the synagogue, or at home when leading th…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קיטל (kitl).

parole.significato: A Jewish folk musician.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קלעזמער (klezmer), from Hebrew כְּלֵי זֶמֶר (kléy zémer, “musical instruments”).

parole.significato: a small private synagogue or circle of religious learning
parole.testo: From Yiddish קלויז (kloyz), from Middle High German klūse (“hermitage”, by extension “snug, narrow dwelling”), from Old High German klūsa, from Proto-West Germanic *klūsā, from Latin clūsa (“something closed”). Cognate with German Klause, Dutch kluis, Old English clūse.

parole.significato: A clumsy or stupid person.
parole.testo: From Yiddish קלאָץ (klots, literally “wooden beam”); cognate to German Klotz (“block, lump”). Doublet of clot and clod.

parole.significato: A type of dumpling made of matzo eaten by Ashkenazi Jews during Passover.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קניידל (kneydl), cognate to German Knödel (“dumpling”). Doublet of quenelle.

parole.significato: matzo balls
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קניידלעך (kneydlekh).

parole.significato: An Eastern European Jewish, or Yiddish, snack food consisting of a dumpling covered with a shell of baked or fried dough
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קניש (knish), from Polish knysz and Ukrainian книш (knyš).

parole.significato: Fit for use or consumption, in accordance with Jewish law (especially relating to food).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish כּשר (kosher), from Hebrew כָּשֵׁר (kashér).

parole.significato: A jolting upward slide on violin made by pressing a finger down on the string at the end of a note.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קרעכץ (krekhts, “groan”)

parole.significato: Small dumplings of Eastern European origin, filled with meat or cheese and served usually in soup.
parole.testo: From Yiddish קרעפּלאַך (kreplakh), a regional plural form of קרעפּל (krepl, “meat dumpling”).

parole.significato: A traditional savoury or sweet Jewish dish consisting of a baked pudding of pasta, potatoes, or rice, with vegetables,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קוגל (kugl), from Middle High German kugel(e) (“ball”), referring to the roundish appearance of some puddings. Further etymology uncertain; see German Kugel for more.

parole.significato: To feel delighted and proud; to boast; to gloat.
parole.testo: From Yiddish קוועלן (kveln), from Middle High German quellen, from Old High German quellan, from Proto-West Germanic *kwellan. Cognate with German quellen and English quell (“source, spring”).

parole.significato: To whine or complain, often needlessly and incessantly.
parole.testo: From Yiddish קוועטשן (kvetshn, literally “to squeeze, pinch”), from Middle High German quetschen (“crush, press”).

parole.significato: A person who kvetches; a complainer, kvetch.
parole.testo: From kvetch + -er, or borrowed from Yiddish קוועטשער (kvetsher).

parole.significato: A note with a (general or specific) petitionary prayer, used in Hasidic Judaism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish קוויטל (kvitl).

parole.significato: People from the same town, in American Jewish communities.
parole.testo: From Yiddish לאַנדסלײַט (landslayt). See לאַנד (land) and לײַט (layt).

parole.significato: A person who does not go to sea, who lacks the skills of a sailor or who is uncomfortable on ships or boats.
parole.testo: From land + -s- + man. In meanings 3 and 4, influenced by Yiddish לאַנדסמאַן (landsman). Compare also German Landsmann, Norwegian landsmann. Doublet of lantzman.

parole.significato: A mutual aid society or benefit society of Jewish immigrants from the same European town or region.
parole.testo: From Yiddish [Term?]; compare German Landsmannschaft.

parole.significato: A fellow Jew who grew up in the same Eastern European shtetl as the speaker.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish לאַנדסמאַן (landsman). Doublet of landsman.

parole.significato: A traditional Jewish black kaftan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish לאַפּסערדאַק (lapserdak). See that entry for more.

parole.significato: A pancake fried in oil, usually made from potatoes and sometimes also onions, traditionally served on Hanukkah.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish לאַטקע (latke), from either Russian ла́тка (látka, “pastry, patch”) or Ukrainian оладка (oladka, “pancake, fritter”). In Polish łatka (“patch”) or placek, placki (“fritter, fritters”).

parole.significato: To don or put on (tefillin (phylacteries)).
parole.testo: Semantic loan from Yiddish לייגן (leygn, “to put, lay”).

parole.significato: excuse the comparison
parole.testo: From Yiddish להבֿדיל (lehavd(i)l), from Hebrew לְהַבְדִּיל (l'havdíl), the infinitive of הִבְדִּיל (hivdíl, “to separate, to distinguish”).

parole.significato: A Jewish honey-sweetened cake, mainly associated with Rosh Hashanah.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish לעקעך (lekekh).

parole.significato: to read from a Torah scroll
parole.testo: From Yiddish לייענען (leyenen, “to read”).

parole.parola: like a hole in one's head
parole.significato: Absolutely not; used to describe how little one needs an undesirable thing or situation.
parole.testo: Calque of Yiddish װי אַ לאָך אין קאָפּ (vi a lokh in kop).

parole.significato: may it not happen to us; an expression that indicates a desire that a previously mentioned negative thing not happen ag…
parole.testo: From Yiddish לא־עלינו (loy oleynu) and Hebrew לֹא עָלֵינוּ (“lit. (may it) not [be] upon us”).

parole.significato: Flat egg noodles from Yiddish cuisine.
parole.testo: From Yiddish לאָקשן (lokshn).

parole.significato: Salmon that is cured in brine and then smoked at a low temperature so that the flesh remains uncooked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish לאַקס (laks, “salmon”). Doublet of lax.

parole.significato: A meaningless or unproductive job, which contributes little or no value to society.
parole.testo: From Yiddish לופֿט געשעפֿט (luft gesheft), from German Luftgeschäft, from Luft (“air”) + Geschäft (“business”); with spelling influenced by the orthography of the German term.

parole.significato: A person who is highly intellectual or contemplative but detached from practical affairs, especially the need to earn a…
parole.testo: From Yiddish לופֿטמענטש (luftmentsh), from לופֿט (luft, “air”) + מענטש (mentsh, “person”). Compare German von Luft und Liebe leben (“to disregard the practical matters of life”, literally “to live on air and love”), German Luftikus (“impractical, quixotic, or careless person”). The word first appear

parole.significato: A finger.
parole.testo: Apparently from Yiddish לאַפּע (lape)

parole.significato: An important person, often in the negative sense of self-important; a bigwig.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מאַכער (makher, “influential person”, literally “one who makes”) from מאַכן (makhn, “to make”). Cognate, naturally, to English maker and German Macher.

parole.significato: Something large or elaborate.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מגילה (megile, “a lengthy document, a long story”), from Hebrew מגילה / מְגִלָּה (məḡillāh, “a scroll”). Doublet of megillah.

parole.significato: really, very, truly
parole.testo: From Yiddish ממש (mamesh) and Hebrew מַמָּשׁ (mamásh).

parole.significato: The Yiddish language.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מאַמע־לשון (mame-loshn), meaning "mother tongue".

parole.significato: Jewish food consisting of crisp mini croutons used as a soup accompaniment.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מאַנדלאַך (mandlakh, literally “little almonds”).

parole.significato: Small crunchy balls often used as an accompaniment to soup in Jewish cuisine.
parole.testo: From Yiddish. Compare German Mandeln.

parole.significato: alcoholic drink, booze.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish משקה (mashke), derived from Hebrew מַשְׁקֶה (“drink, beverage”).

parole.significato: Thin, unleavened bread in Jewish cuisine.
parole.testo: When stressed on the first syllable, from Yiddish מצה (matse), from Hebrew מַצָּה (matsá); pronunciations stressed on the second syllable are borrowed directly from Hebrew.

parole.significato: An expert in a given field; also, a person who is interested in and knowledgeable about a particular activity or thing;…
parole.testo: From Yiddish מבֿין (meyvn, “connoisseur, expert, know-it-all”), from Hebrew מֵבִין (mevín, “one who understands, connoisseur, expert”), from הֵבִין (hevín, “to understand”). parole.significato: lucky, fortunate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish מזלדיק (mazldik, “lucky”), from Hebrew מַזָּל (“constellation, luck, fortune”). Compare English mazel tov.

parole.significato: Used to express congratulations or good wishes, especially at weddings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish מזל־טובֿ (mazl tov), from Hebrew מַזָּל (mazál, “star, constellation; fate, luck”), from Akkadian 𒌓𒁕 (manzaltum) + Hebrew טוֹב (tov, “good”); literally “good stars, good luck”.

parole.significato: Cash, money.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מזומן (mezumen, “cash”), from Hebrew מְזוּמָּן (m'zumán, “prepared, ready; cash”), passive present participle of זִימֵּן (zimén, “to prepare, appoint”).

parole.significato: A pleasure; a joy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish מחיה (mekhaye), originally from Hebrew מְחַיֶּה (mekhayéh, “he revives”).

parole.significato: A person of strength, integrity, and honor or compassion; a gentleman.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מענטש (mentsh, “an honorable person”), from Middle High German mensch, mensche, mennische, from Old High German mennisko (“man, human being”), from Proto-Germanic *manniskaz (“human”). The spelling mensch was influenced by German Mensch; compare the alternative spellings. Doublet of men

parole.significato: A hypothetical particle that could explain cold fusion.
parole.testo: From meshugge + -on, from Yiddish משוגע (meshuge, “crazy”). Coined by Hungarian-American physicist Edward Teller in 1989 during a Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI)-National Science Foundation (NSF) workshop.

parole.significato: crazy, mad, senseless, insane
parole.testo: From Yiddish משוגע (meshuge, “crazy”), from Hebrew מְשׁוּגָּע (m'shugá, “crazy”), a form of שׁוּגַּע (shugá, “be driven mad”) and שִׁיגַּע (shigá, “drive mad”). First came into use in English around 1880.

parole.significato: crazy, insane
parole.testo: From Yiddish משוגענער (meshugener, “lunatic”, noun). Compare Yiddish משוגע (meshuge, “crazy”).

parole.significato: An ugly person.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מיאוסקייט (mieskeyt, “an ugly person”).

parole.significato: Dairy, containing anything derived from milk.
parole.testo: From Yiddish מילכיק (milkhik) with the spelling influenced by German, or else borrowed directly from German milchig (“milky”). Doublet of milky.

parole.significato: Madness; silliness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish משוגעת (meshugas), from משוגע (meshuge, “crazy”), from Hebrew משוגע (meshugga`, “crazy”), from שׁוּגַּע (shugga‘, “be driven mad”), שִׁיגַּע (shigga‘, “drive mad”).

parole.significato: An (extended) family or clan.
parole.testo: From Yiddish משפּחה (mishpokhe), from Hebrew מִשְׁפָּחָה (mishpakhá, “family”).

parole.significato: An opponent of Hasidism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish מתנגד (misnaged), from Hebrew מִתְנַגֵּד (mitnagéd, “opponent”).

parole.significato: A lot of money.
parole.testo: Probably from motza, a variant of matzo, or its etymon Yiddish מצה (matse, “(unleavened) bread”). Compare bread, dough (“money”).

parole.significato: A feeling of contentment at another person's successes.
parole.testo: From Yiddish נחת (nakhes), from Hebrew נַחַת (nákhat, “contentment”).

parole.significato: foolish, silly
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish נאַריש (narish). Cognate with German närrisch.

parole.significato: foolishness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish נאַרישקייט (narishkeyt).

parole.significato: One who is fearful, indecisive and timid, especially in making decisions and plans, in discussions, debates, arguments,…
parole.testo: From American Yiddish נעביש (nebish), from נעבעך (nebekh, “poor, unfortunate”).

parole.significato: Food.
parole.testo: From Yiddish נאַשן (nashn), from Middle High German naschen (“nibble”) (which is also the parent of German naschen), from Old High German naskōn (“to nibble; parasite”), from Proto-West Germanic *hnaskwōn (“to weaken; make soft; tenderise”). Doublet of nesh.

parole.significato: An exclamation of surprise, emphasis, doubt, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish נו (nu). Doublet of now.

parole.significato: A person who is very annoying; a pest, a nag, a jerk.
parole.testo: From Yiddish נודניק (nudnik), from the root of נודיען (nudyen, “to bore”) + ־ניק (-nik, noun-forming suffix) (English -nik), both of Slavic origin. parole.significato: A whiner; a complainer.
parole.testo: From Yiddish נודזש (nudzh, “an annoying, bothersome person”), from Polish nudzić (“to bore”).

parole.significato: It is highly doubtful: indicating that something is not likely to happen to the person specified.
parole.testo: Calque of Yiddish מען זאָל זיין אזוי מזלדיק (men zol zeyn azoy mazldik, “one should be so lucky”)

parole.significato: Money.
parole.testo: From Yiddish אויפֿן טיש (oyfn tish) in the phrase געלט אויפֿן טיש (gelt oyfn tish, “money on the table”).

parole.significato: Having lots of money rich, wealthy.
parole.testo: From oof + -y. Oof is a clipping of ooftish, from Yiddish אויפֿן טיש (oyfn tish, “on the table”) in the phrase געלט אויפֿן טיש (gelt oyfn tish, “money on the table”).

parole.significato: An exclamation typically expressing mild frustration or expressing feelings of uncertainty or concern.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish אוי (oy, “oh, oy”).

parole.significato: oh my God
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish אוי געוואַלט (oy gevalt).

parole.significato: oh dear
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish אוי וויי (oy vey, literally “oh woe”), from Middle High German ōwē, from ō + wē, the latter being from Old High German wē, from Proto-Germanic *wai, from Proto-Indo-European *wai. Cognate with German o weh, Dutch oh wee, Latin vae, and Esperanto ho ve.

parole.significato: Calves'-foot jelly, a traditional Ashkenazi Jewish dish.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּטשאַ (ptsha), apparently from Turkish paça çorbası (literally “leg soup”).

parole.significato: A poster put up in an Orthodox Jewish community, especially a Haredi enclave, to advise on correct behaviour.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּאַשקעוויל (pashkevil).

parole.significato: To rule, decide, opine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּסקענען (paskenen).

parole.significato: A nasty or contemptible person.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּאַסקודניאַק (paskudnyak), traceable to Polish and Ukrainian.

parole.significato: A seasoned smoked cut of beef, traditionally made from a navel cut.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּאַסטראַמע (pastrame), from Romanian pastramă, from Ottoman Turkish باصدرمه (modern Turkish pastırma), a variation of bastırma (“dried meat”), from root bas- (“to press”). It is sometimes claimed that the origin of the Turkish word is Greek παστώνω (pastóno, “I salt”), from An

parole.significato: Permissible to eat on Passover.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּסחדיק (peysekhdik).

parole.significato: An expression of disgust, rejection, or disappointment.
parole.testo: Probably from Yiddish פֿוי (foy), from German pfui, influenced by phoo.

parole.significato: Somebody who is inept at a task or new to a job.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּישער (pisher, “pisser”), from פּישן (pishn, “to urinate”).

parole.significato: To become aggravated.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּלאַצן (platsn, “to split, crack, burst, explode”).

parole.significato: A flat bread roll, either crisp or chewy, somewhat similar to a bagel
parole.testo: Yiddish פּלעצל (pletsl, “small bread”)

parole.significato: To flop down wearily.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּלאַצן (platsn, “to split, crack, burst, explode”).

parole.significato: A riot aimed at persecution or massacre of a particular ethnic or religious group (usually Jews).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּאָגראָם (pogrom), from Russian погро́м (pogróm).

parole.significato: A wealthy landowner who controls a shtetl.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּריץ (porets, “landowner”), from Hebrew פׇּרִיץ (pārīṣ, “bandit”). Compare Polish puryc.

parole.significato: Invalid for ceremonial or official purposes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּסול (posl), from Hebrew פָּסוּל (pasúl).

parole.significato: A slap or spank. Alternative spellings include patsh, potsh.
parole.testo: From Yiddish פּאַטש (patsh, “slap”).

parole.significato: to work in an amateur fashion for little gain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּאַטשקען (patshken, “to daub, smear”).

parole.significato: Expresses inspiration, amazement, or respect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּששש (pshshsh).

parole.significato: The face (front part of the head).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּנים (ponem), from Hebrew פָּנִים (paním, “face”).

parole.significato: A (usually comic) theatrical reenactment of the book of Esther.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּורימשפּיל (purimshpil).

parole.significato: A small coin receptacle for charitable donations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּושקע (pushke, “tin can, tzedakah box”), from Polish puszka (“can”). Ultimately a doublet of box and pyxis.

parole.significato: A fool, an idiot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פּאָץ (pots, “penis, fool”); compare similar semantic developments in futz.

parole.significato: Mercy, compassion, pity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish רחמנות (rakhmones, “mercy”).

parole.significato: a rabbi
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish רבֿ (rov).

parole.significato: Shortened form of Rebbe.
parole.testo: From Yiddish רב (reb).

parole.significato: The spiritual leader of a Hasidic Jewish community.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish רבי (rebe). Doublet of rabbi.

parole.significato: The wife of a rabbi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish רביצין (rebetsin), from Hebrew רב (“master”) plus Slavic *-itsa (feminine suffix) plus Yiddish ־ין (-in, feminine suffix).

parole.significato: A type of Jewish pastry, which may be filled with various fruit, nuts, chocolate, etc.
parole.testo: From Yiddish ראָגאַל (rogal) with plural suffix ־לעך (-lekh), from Polish rogal (“crescent roll”).

parole.significato: A person honoured at a Jewish brit milah by holding the baby boy in his lap as the mohel performs the circumcision.
parole.testo: From Yiddish סנדק (sandek), from Hebrew סַנְדָּק (sandák), most likely from Ancient Greek σύντεκνος (súnteknos, literally “companion of child”), from συν- (sun-) + τέκνον (téknon).

parole.significato: A member of the Satmar movement.
parole.testo: From Yiddish סאַטמאַר (satmar), from Hungarian Szatmár, the name of the city now known as Satu Mare. Doublet of Satu Mare.

parole.significato: A member of the Satmar movement.
parole.testo: From Yiddish סאַטמאַרער (satmarer).

parole.significato: A kind of borscht made with sorrel (or occasionally lemongrass).
parole.testo: From Yiddish שטשאַוו (shtshav), from Polish szczaw.

parole.significato: A loser or a fool.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שלימיל (shlimil).

parole.significato: To carry, drag, or lug.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שלעפּן (shlepn, “to drag”), from Middle High German slepen, from Middle Low German slêpen, from or related to Old High German sleifen (“to drag”) and slifan (“to slip”), from Proto-West Germanic *sleupan. Compare German schleppen (“to haul”) and its inherited doublet schleifen (“to drag

parole.significato: One who wanders aimlessly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שלעפּער (shleper).

parole.significato: A chronically unlucky person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שלימזל (shlimazl), from Middle High German slim (“crooked”) and Hebrew מזל (mazzāl, “luck”)

parole.significato: Any commodity that is shoddy or inferior; now, usually, writing or audiovisual content that is shoddy or inferior.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שלאַק (shlak), related to German Schlag (“blow, strike, hit”).

parole.significato: Software that is of shoddy or inferior quality.
parole.testo: From schlock (“shoddy or inferior commodity”) + -ware, from Yiddish שלאַק (shlak).

parole.significato: A person who is clumsy, oafish, socially awkward, unattractive or unkempt.
parole.testo: From Yiddish זשלאָב (zhlob, “goyish bumpkin, redneck”), derived from Polish żłób (“manger, trough; furrow, large groove in the soil”). Compare Russian жлоб (žlob). Originated in Eastern Europe as part of klezmer musician cant (Klezmer-loshn). In its original sense, the word only applied to non-Jewis

parole.significato: Clumsy, oafish, or socially awkward; unattractive or unkempt.
parole.testo: From schlub + -y; schlub is derived from Yiddish זשלאָב (zhlob), perhaps from Polish żłób (“manger, trough; furrow, large groove in the soil”).

parole.significato: Someone who is lazy, slovenly, or dull-looking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שלומפּ (shlump, “stupid, foolish, or inept person”). Compare obsolete German Schlumpe (modern Schlampe).

parole.significato: Used to form a reduplicated rhyming compound of any word in order to express disparagement, dismissal, or derision.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמ־ (shm-), imitative of many Yiddish words such as schmaltz or schmuck.

parole.significato: Rendered chicken or goose fat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמאַלץ (shmalts) or German Schmalz. Doublet of smalt, smalto, and enamel.

parole.significato: A spread that goes on a bagel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמיר (shmir, “smear, spread”); compare German schmieren. Doublet of smear, smearcase. By surface analysis, schm- + smear. The sense “bribe” is from Yiddish שמירן (shmirn, “to smear, to bribe”), senses found also in German schmieren. The implication is that a bribe helps “lubric

parole.significato: A penis.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמעקל (shmekl), a diminutive of Yiddish שמאָק (shmok), from which schmuck is borrowed.

parole.significato: An idiot; a jerk.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמעגעגע (shmegege).

parole.significato: A stupid person; a fool; a nincompoop.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמענדריק (shmendrik), from the name of a character in the operetta Shmendrik, oder di komishe Chaseneh (Schmendrik, or The Comical Wedding; שמענדריק, אָדער, די קאָמישע חתונה) by Avrom Goldfaden.

parole.significato: A stupid, obnoxious, pathetic, or otherwise contemptible person; a schmuck.
parole.testo: From Yiddish, alteration of schmuck. Compare also Russian чмо (čmo, “jerk, schmuck”).

parole.significato: To talk casually, especially in order to gain an advantage or make a social connection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמועס (shmues), from Hebrew שְׁמוּעוֹת (sh'mu'ót), plural of שְׁמוּעָה (sh'mu'á, “report, piece of news, rumor”). Cognate with German schmusen (“to cuddle”, older “to flirt, flatter, schmooze”).

parole.significato: A jerk; a person who is unlikable, detestable, or contemptible because they are stupid, foolish, clumsy, oafish, inept,…
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמאָק (shmok, “penis, fool”).

parole.significato: Clothing.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמאַטע (shmate, “rag”).

parole.significato: dirt, filth
parole.testo: From Yiddish שמוץ (shmuts) or German Schmutz. Doublet of smut.

parole.significato: A person who is easily taken advantage of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שנוק (shnuk, “person easily imposed upon or cheated”).

parole.significato: to scrounge, sponge, cadge
parole.testo: From Yiddish שנאָרן (shnorn), cf. German schnorren.

parole.significato: beggar
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שנאָרער (shnorer) or German Schnorrer.

parole.significato: Nose.
parole.testo: Likely from Yiddish שנויץ (shnoyts), cognate to German Schnauze (“snout”) and English snout. Compare schnozzle. A less common theory suggests a variant of nose influenced by schm-, or by general association with Yiddish words. Attested since at least 1940.

parole.significato: The human nose, especially one that is large.
parole.testo: Probably from Yiddish שנויץ (shnoyts, “snout”), cognate to German Schnauze (“snout, muzzle”) and English snout. The Oxford English Dictionary suggests the word may be pseudo-Yiddish coined in English. Attested since 1930.

parole.significato: A bit, morsel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שטיקל (shtikl).

parole.significato: wit, sense, gumption
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שׂכל (seykhl, “wit, sense, common sense”), from Hebrew שֵׂכֶל (sekhel, “intelligence”).

parole.significato: Shabbat or shabbat (the biblical seventh-day Sabbath).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שבת (shabes), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát). Doublet of Shabbat and Sabbath.

parole.significato: A gentile who performs certain acts which are forbidden to observant Jews on Shabbat, such as kindling fire.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שבת גוי (shabes goy, literally “Sabbath gentile”).

parole.significato: marriage broker, matchmaker
parole.testo: From Yiddish שדכן (shadkhn), from Hebrew שַׁדְכָן.

parole.significato: A question, especially a religious or legal one posed to a rabbi regarding Jewish law (halacha).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שאלה (sheyle), Hebrew שְׁאֵלָה (sh'elá, “question”).

parole.significato: Shame; disgrace.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שאַנדע (shande), from Middle High German schande, schante, from Old High German scanta, skanta, from Proto-West Germanic *skandu (“shame”). Doublet of shand.

parole.significato: to perform shechita, to ritually slaughter
parole.testo: From Yiddish שעכטן (shekhtn), from Hebrew שָׁחַט (shakhát) (Ashkenazi Hebrew: Shókhat).

parole.significato: A Jew.
parole.testo: Seems to have originated in 1820s London. Could be a mockery of Yiddish שיין (sheyn, “beautiful, nice”), much used in praising wares.

parole.significato: A gentile, a non-Jewish male.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שייגעץ (sheygets), from Hebrew שֶׁקֶץ (šeqeṣ, “abomination”).

parole.significato: A wig worn by married Orthodox Jewish women.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שייטל (sheytl), cognate to German Scheitel (“parting”).

parole.significato: A state of chaos or confusion.
parole.testo: UK late-19th century. Borrowed from Yiddish שלימזל (shlimazl, “misfortune”), from Middle High German slim (“crooked”) and Hebrew מַזָּל (mazzāl, “luck”). Cognate with US English schlimazel (“unlucky person”). Compare German Schlamassel.

parole.significato: Drunk, drunkard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שיכּור (shiker, “drunk”), from Hebrew שיכור / שִׁכּוֹר (shikór).

parole.significato: Drunk.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שיכּור (shiker, “drunk”), from Hebrew שיכּור.

parole.significato: A system of matchmaking in which Jewish singles are introduced to each other.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שידוך (shídekh), deriving from Hebrew שִׁדּוּךְ (shidúkh, “matchmaking”).

parole.significato: A non-Jewish girl, especially one who is attractive and young.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שיקסע (shikse), which is partly derived from the Hebrew שֶׁקֶץ (šeqeṣ, “abomination, impure, object of loathing”).

parole.significato: good job
parole.testo: From Yiddish שכּ׳ח (shkoyekh), a shortened form of Yiddish יישר כּוח (yasher koyekh), from Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, meaning "may He (God) strengthen your strength".

parole.significato: A rag.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמאַטע (shmate); originally from Polish szmata.

parole.significato: a penis
parole.testo: Borrowing from Yiddish שמעקל (shmekl), diminutive of שמאָק (shmok), “penis; contemptible person”. Compare schmuck.

parole.significato: A losing streak, especially a hitless period in baseball.
parole.testo: From Yiddish

parole.significato: observant of the laws of Shabbat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שומר שבת (shomer shabes), Hebrew שׁוֹמֵר שַׁבָּת.

parole.significato: A Jew.
parole.testo: From Yiddish [Term?] (“small trader”).

parole.significato: A state of impatience, agitation, or anxiety.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שפּילקעס (shpilkes, “needles”), ultimately from a Slavic term such as Polish szpilka, which comes from Italian spilla, from Late Latin spīnula (“little thorn”).

parole.significato: A partial wig that reveals the wearer's hair only at the front, worn by some married Hasidic women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שפּיצל (shpitsl).

parole.significato: An extremely ugly person.
parole.testo: From the fictional ogre Shrek, created by the American author William Steig for his 1990 picture book Shrek! and popularized by the DreamWorks computer-animated movie franchise, whose name derives from Yiddish שרעק (shrek, “fright”).

parole.significato: to stem, to originate, to come from
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שטאַמען (shtamen, “to stem (from), to come (from), to originate (from)”). Doublet of stem.

parole.significato: A scale in Ashkenazi liturgical music.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שטייגער (shteyger).

parole.significato: A Jewish village or small town, especially one in Eastern Europe.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שטעטל (shtetl, “small town, village”), from שטאָט (shtot, “city”) + ־ל (-l, “diminutive suffix”) (compare German Städtl, Swabian Städtele), from Old High German stat, from Proto-West Germanic *stadi, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis. Doublet of stead.

parole.significato: A generally humorous routine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שטיק (shtik, “shtick, act, piece”). Cognate with German Stück, Dutch stuk. Doublet of shtuka, steck, and styca.

parole.significato: A small, informal synagogue or shul.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שטיבל (shtibl, “small room/house, informal synagogue”), diminutive of שטוב (shtub) + ־ל (-l) from Old High German stuba, from Proto-West Germanic *stubu.

parole.significato: collaborator; traitor; informer
parole.testo: From Yiddish שטינקער (shtinker).

parole.significato: A fur hat, usually worn by some married Haredi Jewish men on Shabbat and during Jewish holidays and other festive occas…
parole.testo: Yiddish שטרײַמל (shtrayml).

parole.significato: Silent; speechless; dumb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שטום (shtum, “mute, dumb, voiceless”), from Middle High German stum, from Old High German stum, from Proto-West Germanic *stumm. Cognate with German stumm, Dutch stom, Swedish stum. Doublet of stum.

parole.significato: push
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שטופּן (shtupn), perhaps related to German stupsen (“nudge”), or possibly German stopfen (“stuff”).

parole.significato: nonsense, stupidity
parole.testo: From Yiddish שטות (shtus), from Hebrew שְׁטוּת (sh'tút).

parole.significato: To sway back and forth during Jewish prayer.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שאָקלען (shoklen). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skukkijaną.

parole.significato: An Ashkenazi synagogue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שול (shul, “school, synagogue”), from Old High German scuola (“school”), from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ). Doublet of schola and school.

parole.significato: One who attends shul (“a synagogue”); a practising Jew.
parole.testo: From shul (“Ashkenazi synagogue”) + goer. Shul is borrowed from Yiddish שול (shul, “school; synagogue”), from Old High German scuola (“school”), from Latin schola (“school”), from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “place for giving lectures, lecture hall, school”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *se

parole.significato: The penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שוואַנץ (shvants, “tail, penis”).

parole.significato: A person of sub-Saharan African descent; a black person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שוואַרצע (shvartse), feminine and plural form of שוואַרץ (shvarts, “black”). The generalization of the form was likely reinforced by the frequent use referring to black female domestic workers, although forms in -e/-a and -er would have merged in any case in a non-rhotic accent

parole.significato: A mother-in-law.
parole.testo: From Yiddish שוויגער (shviger).

parole.significato: Sweat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שוויצן (shvitsn), from Old High German swizzen (Modern German schwitzen), from Proto-Germanic *swait- (English sweat), from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”). Doublet of sweat.

parole.significato: joy
parole.testo: From Yiddish שׂמחה (simkhe), from Hebrew שִׂמְחָה (simkhá, literally “happiness”).

parole.significato: To take part in the shiva mourning ritual.
parole.testo: Partial calque of Yiddish שבֿעה זיצן (shive zitsn, “to sit shiva”).

parole.significato: A tall hat made of black fur, traditionally worn by Hassidic Polish Jews.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ספּאָדיק (spodik), from Polish spodek (“saucer”).

parole.significato: A Jewish aunt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish טאַנטע (tante), from German Tante, from French tante.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Tash Hassidic community.
parole.testo: From Tash + -er. From Yiddish טאַהש (tosh), from Hebrew טאהש.

parole.significato: A small ornament of minor value; a knick-knack, a trinket.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish טשאַטשקע (tshatshke, “ornament; trinket; toy; (figurative) attractive girl or woman”), from a Slavic language and probably ultimately imitative of a baby’s utterances. Slavic cognates * Polish cacko (“toy; knick-knack, trinket; pretty thing”), from caca (“nice thing”), and czac

parole.significato: Small knotted pastries boiled in a honeyed syrup, a traditional Ashkenazi Jewish treat.
parole.testo: From Yiddish טייגלעך (teyglekh), plural of טייגל (teygl).

parole.significato: A headscarf often worn by married orthodox Jewish women in compliance with the code of modesty known as tzniut, though…
parole.testo: From Yiddish טיכל (tikhl), compare German Tuch (“cloth”).

parole.significato: A festive meal for a religious event, especially Shabbat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish טיש (tish, “table”). Doublet of desk, dais, disc, dish, and discus.

parole.significato: to immerse (something, especially kitchenware) into a mikveh
parole.testo: From Yiddish טובֿלן (toyvln), from Hebrew טוֹבֵל (tovél), present tense of טָבַל (tavál).

parole.significato: A Jewish merchant in Edinburgh area in the first half of the XX century.
parole.testo: From traveller, probably through Yiddish or Scots.

parole.significato: Not kosher.
parole.testo: From Yiddish טרייף (treyf), from Hebrew טְרֵפָה (trefá).

parole.significato: A cymbalom, or hammered dulcimer, used in klezmer music.
parole.testo: From Yiddish צימבל (tsimbl). Doublet of cymbal.

parole.significato: Problems or troubles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish צרות (tsores), plural of צרה (tsore, “trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (tsará, “trouble, tragedy, calamity”).

parole.significato: The buttocks, rear end, butt.
parole.testo: From Yiddish תּחת (tokhes, “buttocks”), in turn from Hebrew תַּחַת (tákhat, “buttocks”).

parole.significato: An employee, usually male, of a Borscht Belt resort charged with the duty of entertaining guests throughout the day by…
parole.testo: Circa 1930, from Yiddish טומלער (tumler). Related to English tumble, and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tūmōną (“to turn, rotate”).

parole.significato: The buttocks.
parole.testo: Short for toches, from Yiddish תחת (tokhes), from Hebrew תַּחַת (taḥaṯ, “bottom”).

parole.significato: Buttocks, bottom.
parole.testo: From tuchus, from Yiddish תּחת (tokhes), from Hebrew תַּחַת (tákhat, “underside, buttocks”).

parole.significato: A stew of fruit or vegetables traditionally served on Rosh Hashanah.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish צימעס (tsimes).

parole.significato: The night before brit milah.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish וואך־נאכט (vakh-nakht)

parole.significato: An unspecified object; a thingy or doodad.

catena.termine: weben + fetzen

parole.testo: A nonsense word, popularized by MAD Magazine in 1953. Generally accepted to be a derivation from Yiddish [Term?], from German weben + fetzen.

parole.significato: shitty, crappy
parole.testo: From Yiddish פֿאַרקאַקטע (farkakte), inflected form of פֿאַרקאַקט (farkakt, “shitty, turned into shit, shat upon”). Compare synonymous German verkackt. The English forms with v- are influenced by the German spelling of the prefix ver-.

parole.significato: Overcome with emotion, choked up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish פֿאַרקלעמט (farklemt, “depressed, distraught; choked up”). The English spelling was influenced by the German prefix ver- corresponding to Yiddish פֿאַר־ (far-). parole.significato: Synonym of vigorish (“charge taken on bets”).
parole.testo: Clipping of vigorish, from Yiddish וויגריש (vigrish), from Russian вы́игрыш (výigryš, “winnings”).

parole.significato: A charge taken on bets, as by a bookie or gambling establishment.
parole.testo: From Yiddish וויגריש (vigrish), from Russian вы́игрыш (výigryš, “winnings”).

parole.significato: joke
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish וויץ (vitz, “joke”). Compare German Witz and English wit.

parole.significato: Marijuana; cannabis, especially used as a drug.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish וואַנץ (vants, “bedbug”), by analogy to the English slang term roach. Attested since the 1950s.

parole.significato: A short Torah lesson, thought, or insightful saying, often shared at a wedding, gathering, or celebration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish וואָרט (vort, “word”). Doublet of word.

parole.significato: The anniversary of a person's death, usually a parent's, often marked by the lighting of a memorial candle and other ri…
parole.testo: PIE word  *yóh₁r̥ Borrowed from Yiddish יאָרצײַט (yortsayt), from Middle High German jārzīt (“anniversary; Christian commemoration of a person’s death”); from Middle High German jār (“year”) (from Old High German jār (“year”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yéh₁-r/n- (“year”)) + Middle High Ge

parole.significato: A skullcap worn by religious Jewish males (especially during prayer).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish יאַרמלקע (yarmlke), from Polish jarmułka (“skullcap”), from Turkic; compare Turkish yağmurluk (“rain apparel”).

parole.significato: good job!, well done!
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish יישר כּוח (yasher koyekh)

parole.significato: A Jew of German-speaking origin.
parole.testo: From Yiddish יעקע (yeke). See Wikipedia.

parole.significato: Relating to the Yekkes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish יעקיש (yekish), equivalent to Yekke + -ish.

parole.significato: The world to come, hereafter
parole.testo: From Yiddish יענע וועלט (yene velt, “the world to come”, literally “that world”).

parole.significato: A woman who meddles in the business of others; a busybody; a female gossipmonger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish יענטע (yente).

parole.significato: An academy for the advanced study of Jewish texts.
parole.testo: From Yiddish ישיבה (yeshive), from Hebrew יְשִׁיבָה (y'shivá, “sitting”).

parole.significato: noble origins; pedigree
parole.testo: From Yiddish יחוס (yikhus).

parole.significato: A Jew.
parole.testo: From Yiddish ייִד (yid, “Jew”). Doublet of Jew.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Yiddish language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ייִדיש (yidish), from Middle High German jüdisch (in reference to the language, more fully jüdischdiutsch (literally “Jewish-German”)). By surface analysis, Yid + -ish.

parole.significato: A proponent of the Yiddish language and culture.
parole.testo: From Yiddish ייִדישיסט (yidishist, “Yiddishist (person)”). By surface analysis, Yiddish + -ist.

parole.significato: Jewishness; the Jewish way of life, particularly Ashkenazi and Yiddish culture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish ייִדישקייט (yidishkeyt).

parole.significato: Traditional curse, appended to the names of infamous enemies of the Jewish people: May his name be erased.
parole.testo: From Yiddish ימח־שמו (yimákh shmóy, “may his name be obliterated”), in turn from Biblical Hebrew יִמַּח שְׁמוֹ (yīmmaḥ šəmō, “may his name be erased”).

parole.significato: having fulfilled the requirements of a mitzvah
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish יוצא זײַן (yoytse zayn), from Hebrew יוֹצֵא (yotsé), active participle of יָצָא (yatsá, “to exit”).

parole.significato: A foolish, incompetent, awkward, or contemptible person.
parole.testo: From Yiddish, probably from יאָנץ (yonts).

parole.significato: Having a plump and sexually attractive figure; voluptuous, well-proportioned; large.
parole.testo: From Yiddish זאַפֿטיק (zaftik), cognate to German saftig (“juicy”). Doublet of sappy.

parole.significato: grandfather
parole.testo: From Yiddish זיידע (zeyde, “grandfather”).

parole.significato: A punch; a blow.
parole.testo: From Yiddish זעץ (zets, “a punch, a blow, a hit”), ultimately from Old High German Satz (“a leap”). Compare with Yiddish זעצן (zetsn, “to sit”).
